titleStmt.title: Testimonies to John of Ephesus's Ecclesiastical History, Part 3 from the Chronicle of Michael the Syrian

editionStmt.p: This is a new edition of all passages in the Chronicle of Michael the Syrian which either 1) are introduced as quotations of the third part of the Ecclesiastical History (henceforth EH) of John of Ephesus, or 2) bear a close resemblance to passages found in the EH, or 3) can serve to close gaps in the sole manuscript of the EH. Silvio Roggo identified the passages based on a comparison of the Chronicle to the EH and transcribed them from the manuscript. The list of testimonies found in Jan van Ginkel's dissertation (pp. 237-240) provided an important point of comparison, as did the edition of John of Ephesus's EH by E. W. Brooks. This is a largely diplomatic edition of the Syriac text (available online via vhmml.org) found in the Edessa-Aleppo codex, which has also been published as a facsimile edition by Gregorios Yuhanna Ibrahim in 2009. Emendations have been introduced only on rare occasion. The Syriac text was proofread by Philip Michael Forness.

References have been included to the digitized version of the codex on vhmml.org and to the edition by Jean-Baptiste Chabot. The codex, Ibrahim's facsimile edition, and Chabot's older edition are nearly identical to one another in regard to the columns and lines (except for cases where Chabot omits text deleted in the original manuscript). The only real difference lies in the page numbers, with the codex being numbered according to folios (the numbers being written on the verso side of each folio), and with Ibrahim's page count always being 3 higher than that of Chabot, e.g. Codex 168v.c.15 corresponds to Ibrahim 339.c.15 and to Chabot 336.c.15.

normalization.p: All the abbreviations used by the scribe have been resolved.

The codex seems to use East Syriac vowels for at least pṯāḥā, zqāp̄ā, rḇāṣā, and rḇāṣā karyā. It is unclear whether these vowels were written by the scribe or a later reader, and they have been retained here. The normal diacritical dot has been used for marks that may indicate the vowels ḥḇāṣā, ʿṣāṣā, and ʿṣāṣā rwiḥā on a waw or yoḏ, as it is unclear whether these should be understood as vowels.
Marks for rukkaḵā and quššāyā are occasionally included in red ink, and these have been retained in the present edition.

punctuation.p: The punctuation follows that found in the manuscript. The two-point graphemes ܆ and ܇ have been normalized to be in line with the text, including when one dot is written under the end of the word. The diacritical dot placed above the taw on third feminine singular perfect verbs has been indicated, although the dot does not appear different from other diacritical dots in the manuscript. This is also the case for nouns ending in taw in the construct state that make use of the same diacritical dot.
